summary: Gives corrections to RFC 560, the Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing Telnet option. A fully updated version of the specification was filed in the Protocols Notebook as a separate NIC document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 581 corrects and clarifies the RCTE TELNET option described in RFC 560. It adds a missing option code and message ending, and explains when hosts should send and buffer typed text.

questions: what is the rcte telnet option
what is the rcte option code
what option code does rcte use
subtitle: Corrections and clarifications to the TELNET RCTE option specification.

tldr.problem: RFC 560 omitted the RCTE option code and an end marker in its subnegotiation format, and its transmission rules needed clarification.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 581 supplies option code 7, adds IAC SE to the subnegotiation form, and revises the rules for transmission characters, break characters, buffering and resets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 581 updates RFC 560 and points to a completely updated RCTE specification in the Protocols Notebook as NIC document 19859.

today: The unit records RFC 581's status as Unknown and says it updates RFC 560. The note points to a completely updated RCTE specification in the Protocols Notebook.

sections.title: Option Code and Message Ending
sections.content:
RFC 581 says the RCTE specification omitted the option's name and code from a section; the corrected form is RCTE 7. It also adds the End of Subnegotiation parameter to the subnegotiation format: IAC SB RCTE <cmd> [BC1 BC2] [TC1 TC2] IAC SE.

All examples of RCTE subnegotiation commands should include IAC SE. The sample scenario is also changed to reflect the asynchronous events that can occur with RCTE.
sections.plainLanguage: The option number and a required ending marker were missing from RFC 560. This note supplies them and updates the examples.

sections.title: Transmission and Break Rules
sections.content:
The authors agree with RFC 563's criticism that the earlier wording could prevent network I/O and server computation from overlapping. A Transmission character is changed from a requirement to a recommendation to send accumulated text, using the character classes in effect when the character is typed.

A Break character still requires the Using host to send accumulated text and also suspends printing or discarding the user's input until the Serving host sends a Break Reset. The note also clarifies that echoing is suspended after a Break character until that reset arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: A Transmission character recommends sending the buffered text, while a Break character requires a send and pauses printing until the server resets the break state.

sections.title: Buffering and Reset Coordination
sections.content:
The revised rules impose no mandatory transmission constraints. A Using host may send one character at a time, though the RFC says this wastes RCTE; transmission classes are guidelines. If a buffer fills and more typing would lose text, the user should be notified.

Serving and Using hosts must synchronize Break Class Reset commands with Break characters. The note says text should be buffered until a character in the transmission class active when it was typed. When the transmission classes change, the Using host may rescan buffered text under the new rules or send the buffered text as a group.
sections.plainLanguage: The typing host can send data when needed to avoid losing text, even if a transmission guideline would say to wait. The hosts must coordinate break resets with the characters that trigger them.

references.text: Crocker, D. and Postel, J., Remote Controlled Transmission and Echoing TELNET Option, RFC 560.
